definition: Anachronistic means out of its correct place in time — belonging to a different period, earlier or later, than the one in which it appears.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word anachronistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know anachronistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The mural's one anachronistic touch is beloved anyway: a steam locomotive puffing along behind the medieval harvest, four centuries ahead of the rails.
A dated phrase is merely a step behind the times — a lighter charge than anachronistic, which says the thing belongs to another era altogether.
Fossilized goes further than anachronistic: not just astray in the wrong era, but frozen so completely in a past form that all life and change have left it.

Incongruous means out of place in its surroundings, whatever the reason — a mismatch of kind, style, or mood. Anachronistic is the special case where the mismatch is one of time: the thing belongs to a different era than the scene around it.

Antiquated means so old-fashioned it feels quaint or outmoded, judged against the present's own standards. A thing can be antiquated without ever leaving its era; anachronistic says it has crossed into the wrong one — in either direction, too early or too late.

Halfway through the Civil War film, a critic spotted a jet's contrail crossing the sky behind the cavalry charge — one anachronistic streak of white that no amount of costume research could excuse.
Anachronistic is the exact word because it names something sitting outside its proper time: contrails belong to the age of jet engines, and the film's sky belongs to 1863.
The detail is not wrong in itself — only wrongly placed in time, and that misplacement is precisely what anachronistic points to.

Reach for anachronistic when the problem is placement in time: the thing belongs to a different period than the scene around it, whether it shows up too early or lingers too late — a wristwatch in a Roman epic, a town crier on a modern payroll.
If something is simply behind the times in its own present, antiquated is the honest word, and if the mismatch has nothing to do with time — wrong style, wrong setting — incongruous covers it.
Keep it apart from this unit's ephemeral and transitory, which measure how long a thing lasts, not whether it landed in the right era.

The Marsh House had been restored to the year 1885, down to the horsehair sofa and the oil lamps.
So the docent was puzzled to find visitors smiling at the parlor desk.
On it, gleaming, sat a chrome rotary telephone from the 1950s.
A well-meaning volunteer had donated it, and no one had checked the date.
In an ordinary living room the phone would have been a charming antique; in this parlor it was anachronistic, seventy years ahead of everything around it.
'Every object in a period room makes a promise about time,' the director wrote in her memo.
'This one breaks it.' The phone went to the archive shelf, and a letter-copying press of the correct decade took its place on the desk.
